title: Why Joseph Lister Sprayed Carbolic Acid on Patients
topic: Why Joseph Lister sprayed carbolic acid over his patients during surgery

lines: A surgeon soaked clean towels in harsh acid to save a boy.
Surgery in 1865 was a deadly gamble for every patient.
At one hospital, sixteen out of thirty-five patients died.
Open wounds filled with pus, forcing doctors to cut off limbs.
Then an eleven-year-old boy arrived with a broken leg.
His bone pierced the skin, which usually led to death.
Joseph Lister set the bone and used carbolic acid on the leg.
He wrapped the wound in tin foil for four days.
When Lister checked the skin, he saw no infection.
You see, it was like cleaning smelly sewage with strong chemicals.
Louis Pasteur showed that tiny invisible germs cause decay in open wounds.
Lister realized that destroying these micro-organisms would stop infections.
Carbolic acid wiped out the germs inside open cuts.
Deaths dropped from sixteen in thirty-five down to six in forty.
Burned skin from the acid later forced doctors to create germ-free surgery.

claims.claim: Before antiseptic operations were introduced at the hospital, there were sixteen deaths in thirty-five surgical cases.

On August 12, 1865, Lister treated an eleven-year-old boy with a tibia fracture piercing the skin by setting the bone, applying carbolic acid soaked towels and tin foil for four days, which prevented infection.
Officials in Carlisle experimented with sewage treatment using carbolic acid to reduce the smell, which inspired Lister to try it on wounds.
Lister recognized that putrefaction in wounds is caused by germs, connecting to Louis Pasteur's germ theory.
After antiseptic surgery was introduced, mortality dropped from sixteen deaths in thirty-five cases to six deaths in forty cases.
Skin irritation caused by continual exposure to phenol eventually led to the introduction of aseptic (germ-free) techniques in surgery.
